full_judgment:
A.M. Mahmudur Rahman, J: The petitioners obtained this Rule against the order of the learned Munsif, Mirersarai Upazila, Chittagong setting aside an order of dismissal of the Miscellaneous Case and of restoration of Other Suit No. 20 of 1980. 

 2. The opposite parties Nos. 1 to 3 filed Other Suit No. 20 of 1980 against the petitioners and others for declaration of title to the disputed land and pond on various pleas. The petitioners contested the suit as defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filing two separate written statements denying the material allegations made in the plaint. After service of summons the suit was fixed for hearing on 20.9.1983 and the petitioners filed hajira on that date. But the suit was dismissed for default as the plaintiffs did not appear at the time when the suit was taken up for hearing by the learned Munsif after rejecting the application for adjournment filed by the plaintiffs. Thereafter on 25.9.1983 the plaintiffs filed Misc. Case No. 47 of 1983 under Order 9, rule 9 C.P.C. for setting aside the Order of dismissal and for restoration of the suit. But as the plaintiffs did not put in the requisites and did not take step in the said Miscellaneous case it was dismissed on 10.11.1983. After dismissal of the said case the plaintiffs filed an application under section 151 C.P.C. for restoration of the said Misc. Case. The learned Munsif by his order dated 24.11.1983 allowed the application and set aside the order dated 10.11.1983 dismissing the Miscellaneous Case No. 47 of 1983 and restored the same to its file on condition for payment of cost of Tk. 100/- to the defendants. Thereafter the Misc. Case was heard and the order of dismissal of the suit for default made on 20.9.1983 was set aside and the suit was restored to its file and number on condition to pay cost of Tk. 200/- to the defendant within 7 days. But as the same was not paid within the time by the plaintiffs the learned Munsif by his order dated 11.3.1984 dismissed the Misc. Case No. 47 of 1983. But on the following day i.e. 12.3.1984 the plaintiffs deposited the cost and file an application under section 151 C.P.C. for setting aside the order of dismissal of the Miscellaneous Case passed on 11.3.1984 and for restoration of the suit. The learned Munsif by his order dated 22.3.1984 restored ex-parte the suit on setting aside the order dismissing the Miscellaneous case on condition to pay cost of Tk. 150/- to the defendants. 

 Mr. Nurul Islam Chowdhury only submitted that the order of dismissal of the Misc. Case No. 47 of 1983 filed under Order 9, rule 9 C.P.C. being appealable under Clause (c) of rule (1) of Order 43 C.P.C., the application under section 151 C.P.C. for setting aside the said order and for restoring the suit was not maintainable and the learned Munsif in restoring the suit on setting aside the order of dis-missal of the Miscellaneous Case No. 47 of 1983 acted without jurisdiction and the order also suffers from an error of law occasioning failure of justice. An order passed by a Court under Order 9, rule 9 C.P.C. is no doubt an appealable order under Order 43, rule 1(c) C.P.C. In this case from the facts it appears that the application under section 151 of the Code was filed for restoration of the suit on setting aside the order of dismissal of the Misc. Case which was dismissed not for non-appearance of the plaintiff when the case was taken up for hearing but for not depositing the cost within the time allowed by the Court. The power under section 151 of the Code is not a new one, it is inherent in it by virtue of its duty to do justice between the parties before it and it is within the province of the Court to invoke such power to secure the ends of justice regard being had to the facts and circumstances of a given case. In this case the plaintiffs filed an application under Order 9, Rule 9 C.P.C. and the miscellaneous case was started. By the impugned order the miscellaneous case was allowed and the suit was restored. The Misc. case was not dismissed on 11.3.1984 on the ground of non-appearance but for not putting in the cost. The order made on 11.3.1984 was neither an order rejecting the Misc. case for default nor rejecting the case on merit. In my opinion an appeal under Order 43, rule l(c) is not contemplated for such order although an appeal lies from an order dismissing the case filed under Order 9, rule 9 C.P.C. irrespective of whether it has been made for default or on merit. In this respect it is, in my opinion, necessary to see the meaning of the expression "for the ends of justice" occurring in section 151 C.P.C. The expression "for the ends of justice" is to be examined from various angles and also from facts and circumstances of a given case. In the instant case before me the opposite parties (plaintiffs) were present in Court and obtained the order for setting aside the order dismissing the Misc. case for restoration of the suit itself and the Court restored the Misc. case on condition of payment of cost. The expression "default in payment in cost" is not synonymous with the term "non-appearance when the case was called on for hearing". Where the plaintiffs case under Order 9, rule 9 C.P.C. is allowed but subsequently is dismissed for non-compliance with Court's order in not depositing the cost to the defendants in time and the plaintiff files an application under section 151 C.P.C. for setting aside the said order after depositing the cost, I am of the opinion that in such a situation the Court is competent to exercise its inherent power under section 151 C.P.C. in order to secure the ends of justice. The Court's order for payment of cost was complied with by depositing the cost out of time. The order impugned before me was made for securing the ends of justice as the same was directed to avoid multiplicity of proceeding, prolongation of the proceeding and unnecessary financial hazard and to advance cause of justice. In this context I may refer to the decision in the case of Biswanath Banerjee and others Vs. Amar Nath Mukerjee and others, 1962 Cal. 110. In delivering the judgment of the report P.N.
